questions.question_text:
An internet service provider connects five regional towns with high-speed fibre.
The minimum spanning tree of the town network has a total length of $64\text{ km}$.
If the fibre optic cable costs $\$8500$ per kilometre to install, what is the total cost to connect all five towns?

options.why: Made a place-value error by a factor of 10 in multiplication.
Multiplied by 5 towns instead of the 4 MST edges.
Calculated $64 \times 8000$ instead of $64 \times 8500$.

questions.question_text:
The distance table shows the road distances, in kilometres, between four towns $A, B, C, D$.
$\begin{array}{c|cccc} \text{From/To} & A & B & C & D \\ \hline A & - & 14 & 9 & 16 \\ B & 14 & - & 11 & 8 \\ C & 9 & 11 & - & 12 \\ D & 16 & 8 & 12 & - \end{array}$
What is the minimum length of road required to connect all four towns?

options.why: Selected edge $AB=14$ instead of $CB=11$.
Selected non-adjacent minimal edges that form a disconnected graph.
Summed four edges instead of three spanning tree edges.

questions.question_text:
A park authority is paving walking tracks between five park attractions.
The minimum spanning tree of the track network has a total length of $160\text{ metres}$.
If paving costs $\$150$ per metre, what is the total cost of paving the tracks?

options.why: Added an extra zero in the multiplication.
Divided by 10 instead of multiplying correctly.
Multiplied $120 \times 150$ instead of $160 \times 150$.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is true regarding the relationship between a minimum spanning tree and the shortest path between two specific locations $A$ and $B$ in a network?

options.text: The shortest path between $A$ and $B$ is not necessarily contained in the minimum spanning tree.
The minimum spanning tree always contains the shortest path between every pair of vertices.
options.why: Incorrectly assumed the global minimal connector optimizes every local pair.

options.text: A minimum spanning tree can only connect adjacent vertices in the network diagram.
options.why: Confused graph adjacency with path connectivity in a tree.

options.text: The shortest path between $A$ and $B$ and the minimum spanning tree always have identical edge sets.
options.why: Equated a single path with a complete spanning tree.

questions.solution_text:
$\text{MST objective} = \min(\text{total network weight})$
$\text{Shortest path } (A, B) = \min(\text{path distance between } A \text{ and } B)$
A minimum spanning tree minimises total edge weight across the entire network rather than individual pairwise distances.
The shortest path between $A$ and $B$ is not necessarily contained in the minimum spanning tree.

options.why: Included edge $S_5 S_6=16$ instead of $S_2 S_6=7$ and $S_6 S_1=11$.
Summed all edge weights in the network diagram.
Omitted the edge connecting substation $S_4$.
Included the already-cleared road $CE=3$ in the additional road total.
Selected all outer boundary edges instead of the minimum spanning tree.
Omitted the connection to village $A$.

questions.question_text:
A regional transport authority is constructing railway tracks to connect six towns.
The minimum spanning tree of the network has a total length of $65\text{ km}$.
If track construction costs $\$40\,000$ per kilometre, what is the minimum total cost to link all six towns by rail?

options.why: Divided by 10 or made a place-value error in multiplication.
Multiplied by 6 towns ($6 \times 13 \times 40\,000$) instead of the 5 spanning tree edges.
Used $60\text{ km}$ instead of $65\text{ km}$ in the calculation.
